If you have an alternative path (something completely different from SWE or SWE adjacent) that pays "well", I would like to hear. taurath 6 hours ago | next [–] I had to get back into the industry last year after 4 years off for mental health and caregiving. I was able to get back in - 2 years isn’t that much. But the problem is the front door in hiring is broken. Entirely. I didn’t receive almost ANY replies from hundreds of sent out resumes - I have household names and big public high scale launches and wins on my resume, but no FAANG and no degree. I got 2 job offers. One was through a manager from 8 years prior who was working at a place. One was a recruiter who found me on LinkedIn. I got engagement when someone physically actually knew me, they were actually hiring, and my skills overlapped. My honest advice is to apply places and try that dance, get yourself in front of people, real people, and mainly 1-1. Work everyone you have ever worked with. If you’ve reviewed their PR, they need to know that you need a job. Be kind and genuinely catch up with them if you want to, but they are your PRIMARY resource to get a job and you can’t let shame get in your way. Corporations in general are BROKEN right now in massive ways and the industry is going through a crisis. It will likely become better but whatever you have to do to survive do it. Typically companies thus target "good enough" and for lots of positions there are several candidates that fit that bill. In addition to empathy, let me try to offer some advice as someone observing industry trends from the outside for a while -- especially in the center of the AI insanity that is the Bay Area: The buzzword everyone is looking for is "high-agency." No, not those agents, but yes, those will be essential. Basically employers want someone who will start something from scratch and take it to the finish line all by themselves. So my advice, which others have echoed here: Build something useful -- end-to-end -- from scratch -- with AI -– on your own -- that you can show off as soon as possible. The key point is, "high agency" is by definition not something you can just put on your resume; It is something you show , not tell. Yes, you need to do this even as you go through the absolute hell that is a job search. But trust me, this will a) help get a much better job, and b) help in the long run throughout and beyond your career. This will be the most valuable skill in the near future. A few other thoughts: 0. Get a $100 Pro subscription. Either GPT or Claude, doesn't matter much, but you do want access to Fable or Astra. The volume and variety of things you can get done in that quota is astounding. Codex offers a free quota with Astra if you want to get a sense of things. 1. Target a domain you are already very familiar with. You can draw on your long experience as an engineer, or any personal interests you may have. Say a Math tutoring web app that your students could use. This will sharply cut down the time to MVP. 2. Being an end-to-end thing, this will necessarily be something multi-disciplinary. Think of it as doing a one-person startup, so you're going to be forced to do everythig: design, frontend, backend, infra, and maybe even GTM stuff like marketing. Yes, you may not know most of these things, and obviously won't be great at them, but with AI, everything will be good enough. 3. This conveniently also helps explain the gap in your resume. Nobody needs to know you did this in a few months vs 2 years unless they ask. 4. Even when using AI, keep your hands-on skill warm. Most companies still do old-school leetcode interviews. 5. As an extreme backup this might even become something you monetize yourself. Hope this helps, and all the best! reply erfgh 12 minutes ago | parent | next [–] AI has totally demolished portfolio value. They're mostly interested in things I've already done in the past that involved large amount of users, which automatically filters out all those high agency projects. Getting many users for your projects would be an option, but I see two problems there: - finding users requires a set of skills that is completely orthogonal to software development, so you'd need to learn those skills on the side - finding users is getting harder and harder, as your new project is the 100th release of the day Besides, if you manage to build a good project and find users, you might not need a job at all. But let's say there's a 10% chance that happens. Then there's a 90% chance you go into your first interview as someone who failed to get a project off the ground, which is kind of the opposite of showing high agency. And the odds of success are probably closer to 1% or smaller. reply koiueo 3 minutes ago | parent | prev | next [–] Very wordy but counter productive advice IMO.
